blocks.title: Note
blocks.text: In both cases of ellipses, the major axis is the longer line segment and foci lie on the major axis.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Read the table column by column: the second column is just the first column with the roles of \(x\) and \(y\) swapped. So you only need to learn one column well.
The two forms of each directrix agree: \(\frac{c}{e^2} = \frac{ae}{e^2} = \frac{a}{e}\). The latera recta pass through the foci, which is why their equations are \(x = \pm ae\) (or \(y = \pm ae\)).

The equation \(\frac{(x-h)^2}{a^2} + \frac{(y-k)^2}{b^2} = 1\), with \(a > b\) describes a horizontal ellipse with foci at \(F'(h - c, k)\) and \(F(h + c, k)\), where \(c = \sqrt{a^2 - b^2}\). The centre of the ellipse is at the point \(C(h, k)\) and the vertices are located at \((h \pm a, k)\) on the major axis. The co-vertices are located at \((h, k \pm b)\).

blocks.alt: On a pale yellow panel, a cyan horizontal ellipse with centre C(h, k) on a magenta horizontal major axis and a magenta vertical minor axis; vertices A'(left, unlabelled) and A(h + a, k), foci F'(h - c, k) and F(h + c, k), co-vertices B(h, k + b) and B'(h, k - b), the half-axes marked a and b, and cyan vertical double-arrow directrices x = h - a^2/c and x = h + a^2/c.
blocks.caption: Figure 6.16: horizontal ellipse with centre (h, k) (the book uses the number 6.16 twice; original drawing after the textbook's Figure 6.16)

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: In the book's Figure 6.16 (p. 192) the right focus is labelled \(F'(h + c, k)\); it is \(F(h + c, k)\). The centre is printed \(C'(h.k)\) and the top co-vertex \(B(h.k + b)\), with dots in place of commas; they are \(C(h, k)\) and \(B(h, k + b)\). The right vertex is labelled \(B(h + a, k)\); it is the vertex \(A(h + a, k)\). The number 6.16 is also used for the figure in 6.4.1. Our drawing shows the correct labels.

The equation \(\frac{(x-h)^2}{b^2} + \frac{(y-k)^2}{a^2} = 1\), with \(a > b\) describes a vertical ellipse with foci at \(F'(h, k - c)\) and \(F(h, k + c)\), where \(c = \sqrt{a^2 - b^2}\). The centre of the ellipse is at the point \(C(h, k)\) and the vertices are located at \((h, k \pm a)\) on the major axis. The co-vertices are located at \((h \pm b, k)\).

blocks.alt: On a pale yellow panel, a cyan vertical ellipse with centre C(h, k) on a magenta vertical major axis and a magenta horizontal minor axis; vertices A(h, k + a) and A'(h, k - a), the two foci marked by dots on the major axis, co-vertices B'(h - b, k) and B(h + b, k), the half-axes marked a and b, and magenta horizontal double-arrow directrices y = k + a^2/c and y = k - a^2/c.
blocks.caption: Figure 6.17: vertical ellipse with centre (h, k) (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 6.17)

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Why does \((x - h)\) move the ellipse? In \(\frac{(x-h)^2}{a^2} + \frac{(y-k)^2}{b^2} = 1\), the point \((h, k)\) plays exactly the role that \((0, 0)\) played before. Every point of the old ellipse is moved \(h\) units right and \(k\) units up. Its shape, \(a\), \(b\), \(c\) and \(e\) do not change; only the positions change.
Rule: find each feature as if the centre were the origin, then add \(h\) to the x-coordinate and \(k\) to the y-coordinate.
Watch the signs: \((x + 3)^2\) means \(h = -3\), because \(x + 3 = x - (-3)\).

blocks.title: Example 18
blocks.problem: Find an equation of the ellipse with foci (2, 1), (2, 7), major axis of length 10 and sketch its graph.
steps:
Given: foci (2, 1) and (2, 7); length of the major axis 10.
To find: the equation of the ellipse and its sketch.
Method: the foci show the direction of the major axis and the centre; the length gives \(a\); the centre-to-focus distance gives \(c\); then \(b^2 = a^2 - c^2\), and Theorem 2 gives the equation.

Direction of the major axis
Both foci have the same x-coordinate 2, so they lie on the vertical line \(x = 2\).
\[\Rightarrow \text{Major axis is vertical}\]
Why: the foci always lie on the major axis.

Find \(a\)
\[\text{Major axis length} = 10\]
\[2a = 10 \Rightarrow a = 5\]
Why: the major axis has length \(2a\).

Find the centre
\[\text{Centre} = \left(\frac{2+2}{2}, \frac{1+7}{2}\right)\]
\[= (2, 4)\]
Why: the centre is the midpoint of the foci.

Find \(c\)
Distance from centre to either focus:
\[c = |4 - 1| = 3\]
Why: \(c\) is the distance from the centre to a focus.

Find \(b\)
\[c^2 = a^2 - b^2\]
\[3^2 = 5^2 - b^2\]
\[9 = 25 - b^2\]
\[b^2 = 16 \Rightarrow b = 4\]
Why: this is the relation between \(a\), \(b\) and \(c\) for every ellipse.

Write the equation
With centre \((h, k) = (2, 4)\), major axis vertical, \(a = 5\) and \(b = 4\):
\[\frac{(x-h)^2}{b^2} + \frac{(y-k)^2}{a^2} = 1\]
\[\frac{(x-2)^2}{16} + \frac{(y-4)^2}{25} = 1\]
Why: for a vertical major axis the larger number \(a^2\) goes under the \(y\)-term (Theorem 2).

Sketch
Vertices \((2, 4 \pm 5)\): \(A(2, 9)\) and \(A'(2, -1)\).
Co-vertices \((2 \pm 4, 4)\): \(B(6, 4)\) and \(B'(-2, 4)\).
Plot these with the centre and foci and join the four end points with a smooth oval (Figure 6.18).
Why: four end points and the centre fix the ellipse.

Check:
At \(A(2, 9)\): \(\frac{0}{16} + \frac{25}{25} = 1\). Distances from \(A\) to the foci are \(9 - 7 = 2\) and \(9 - 1 = 8\), sum \(10 = 2a\).

blocks.alt: Example 18 plotted exactly on a pale yellow panel: magenta axes (arrows at both ends) with numbered ticks from -4 to 9 on the x-axis and from -2 to 10 on the y-axis; the cyan ellipse (x - 2)^2/16 + (y - 4)^2/25 = 1 with magenta major axis x = 2 from A'(2, -1) to A(2, 9) and minor axis from B'(-2, 4) to B(6, 4), centre C(2, 4) and foci F(2, 7) and F'(2, 1).
blocks.caption: Figure 6.18: the ellipse of Example 18 (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 6.18)

blocks.title: Example 19
blocks.problem: Find an equation of the ellipse with centre (0, 0), focus (5, 0) and vertex (6, 0). Sketch its graph.
steps:
Given: centre (0, 0), focus (5, 0), vertex (6, 0).
To find: the equation and a sketch.
Method: use symmetry to get the other focus and vertex, read off \(a\) and \(c\), then \(b^2 = a^2 - c^2\).

Other focus and vertex
Focus \((5, 0)\): one focus is to the right; the other focus is \((-5, 0)\) by symmetry.
Vertex \((6, 0)\): one vertex is to the right; the other vertex is \((-6, 0)\).
Why: an ellipse is symmetric about its centre.

Direction of the major axis
All points have same y-coordinate 0, so major axis horizontal.
Why: the foci and vertices lie on the major axis.

Find \(a\) and \(c\)
\[(\pm 6, 0) \Rightarrow a = 6,\ a^2 = 36\]
\[(\pm 5, 0) \Rightarrow c = 5,\ c^2 = 25\]
Why: \(a\) is the centre-to-vertex distance, \(c\) the centre-to-focus distance.

Find \(b\)
\[c^2 = a^2 - b^2\]
\[25 = 36 - b^2\]
\[b^2 = 11 \Rightarrow b = \sqrt{11}\]
Why: the ellipse relation.

Write the equation
Horizontal major axis, centre at origin:
\[\frac{x^2}{a^2} + \frac{y^2}{b^2} = 1\]
\[\frac{x^2}{36} + \frac{y^2}{11} = 1\]
Why: horizontal major axis, so \(a^2 = 36\) goes under \(x^2\).

Sketch
Vertices \((\pm 6, 0)\), co-vertices \((0, \pm\sqrt{11}) \approx (0, \pm 3.3)\), foci \((\pm 5, 0)\) (Figure 6.19).
Why: these points fix the curve.

Check:
\(a^2 - b^2 = 36 - 11 = 25 = c^2\), so the foci are \((\pm 5, 0)\) as given, and \((6, 0)\) satisfies \(\frac{36}{36} + 0 = 1\).

blocks.alt: Example 19 plotted exactly on a pale yellow panel: magenta axes (arrows at the X and Y ends) with a tick at -10 on the x-axis and ticks at 5 and -5 on the y-axis; the cyan ellipse x^2/36 + y^2/11 = 1 with centre O(0, 0), vertices A'(-6, 0) and A(6, 0), foci F'(-5, 0) and F(5, 0), and co-vertices B(0, root 11) and B'(0, -root 11).
blocks.caption: Figure 6.19: the ellipse of Example 19 (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 6.19)

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The book's Figure 6.19 labels both foci with a prime: \(F'(-5, 0)\) and \(F'(5, 0)\). The right focus is \(F(5, 0)\). Our drawing shows the correct label.

blocks.title: Example 20
blocks.problem: Find the centre, foci, eccentricity, vertices and directrices of the ellipse whose equation is \(16x^2 + 9y^2 - 64x + 54y + 1 = 0\). Also sketch its graph.
steps:
Given: \(16x^2 + 9y^2 - 64x + 54y + 1 = 0\).
To find: centre, foci, eccentricity, vertices, directrices and a sketch.
Method: complete the square in \(x\) and in \(y\) to reach the translated standard form, then compare with Theorem 2.

Group and take out the coefficients
\[16x^2 + 9y^2 - 64x + 54y + 1 = 0\]
\[(16x^2 - 64x) + (9y^2 + 54y) + 1 = 0\]
\[16(x^2 - 4x) + 9(y^2 + 6y) + 1 = 0\]
Why: completing the square needs \(x^2\) and \(y^2\) with coefficient 1 inside the brackets.

Divide both sides by 144
\[\frac{16(x-2)^2}{144} + \frac{9(y+3)^2}{144} = 1\]
\[\frac{(x-2)^2}{9} + \frac{(y+3)^2}{16} = 1\]
Why: the standard form has 1 on the right side.

Compare with the standard form
Comparing with \(\frac{(x-h)^2}{b^2} + \frac{(y-k)^2}{a^2} = 1\), we obtain
\[h = 2,\ k = -3,\ b^2 = 9 \Rightarrow b = 3\]
\[a^2 = 16 \Rightarrow a = 4\]
Since \(a > b\) and \(a^2\) is under \(y\)-term, major axis is vertical. Centre: \(C(2, -3)\).
Why: the larger denominator is \(a^2\), and \((y + 3) = (y - (-3))\) gives \(k = -3\).

Find \(c\) and \(e\)
\[c^2 = a^2 - b^2 = 16 - 9 = 7\]
\[c = \sqrt{7}\]
\[e = \frac{c}{a} = \frac{\sqrt{7}}{4}\]
Why: the ellipse relation and the definition of eccentricity.

Vertices
Vertices are \(a = 4\) units above and below centre along vertical axis:
\[A(2, -3 + 4) = A(2, 1)\]
\[A'(2, -3 - 4) = A'(2, -7)\]
Why: the vertices lie on the major axis at distance a from the centre.

Foci
Foci are \(c = \sqrt{7}\) units above and below centre:
\[F(2, -3 + \sqrt{7})\]
\[F'(2, -3 - \sqrt{7})\]
Why: the foci lie on the major axis at distance c from the centre.

Directrices
For vertical major axis, directrices are horizontal lines \(y = k \pm \frac{a}{e}\):
\[y = -3 \pm \frac{4}{\sqrt{7}/4}\]
\[y = -3 \pm \frac{16}{\sqrt{7}}\]
Why: the directrices are perpendicular to the major axis, at distance \(\frac{a}{e}\) from the centre.

Sketch
Plot \(C(2, -3)\), \(A(2, 1)\), \(A'(2, -7)\), co-vertices \((2 \pm 3, -3)\), i.e. \(B'(-1, -3)\) and \((5, -3)\), and the foci; join with a smooth oval (Figure 6.20).
Why: these points fix the curve.

blocks.alt: Example 20 plotted exactly on a pale yellow panel: magenta axes with ticks at -5 and 5 on the x-axis and -5 on the y-axis; the cyan ellipse (x - 2)^2/9 + (y + 3)^2/16 = 1 with magenta major axis x = 2 from A'(2, -7) to A(2, 1) and minor axis from B'(-1, -3) to (5, -3), centre C(2, -3) and foci F(2, -3 + root 7) and F'(2, -3 - root 7).
blocks.caption: Figure 6.20: the ellipse of Example 20 (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 6.20)

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: In the book's Figure 6.20 the label \(F(2, -3 + \sqrt{7})\) is printed beside the point \((5, -3)\), the right end of the minor axis. The focus \(F(2, -3 + \sqrt{7}) \approx (2, -0.35)\) lies on the major axis, just below the \(x\)-axis. Our drawing puts the label at the focus.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: Approximate values help the sketch: \(\sqrt{7} \approx 2.65\), so the foci are about \((2, -0.35)\) and \((2, -5.65)\), and the directrices are about \(y \approx 3.05\) and \(y \approx -9.05\), outside the ellipse as they must be.

blocks.title: Example 21
blocks.problem:
An ellipse has the following properties:
(i) Its major axis is vertical and has a length of 10 units.
(ii) The distance between its foci is 6 units.
(iii) The centre of the ellipse is at the point (3, -2).
Find the standard equation of this ellipse.
steps:
Given: major axis vertical, length 10; distance between foci 6; centre (3, -2).
To find: the standard equation.
Method: get \(a\) and \(c\) from the lengths, then \(b^2 = a^2 - c^2\), then Theorem 2.

(i) Major axis
\[2a = 10 \Rightarrow a = 5 \Rightarrow a^2 = 25\]
Why: the major axis has length \(2a\).

(ii) Distance between the foci
\[2c = 6 \Rightarrow c = 3 \Rightarrow c^2 = 9\]
Why: the foci are \(c\) on each side of the centre, so they are \(2c\) apart.

(iii) Centre
\[(h, k) = (3, -2)\]
Why: given.

Find \(b^2\)
\[c^2 = a^2 - b^2\]
\[9 = 25 - b^2 \Rightarrow b^2 = 25 - 9\]
\[b^2 = 16\]
Why: the relation between \(a\), \(b\) and \(c\).

Write the equation
Since the major axis is vertical, the standard form is \(\frac{(x-h)^2}{b^2} + \frac{(y-k)^2}{a^2} = 1\). Substitute \(h = 3\), \(k = -2\), \(a^2 = 25\) and \(b^2 = 16\):
\[\frac{(x-3)^2}{16} + \frac{(y+2)^2}{25} = 1\]
Why: vertical major axis, so \(a^2\) goes under the \(y\)-term; \(y - (-2) = y + 2\).

Check:
Foci \((3, -2 \pm 3)\), i.e. \((3, 1)\) and \((3, -5)\), are \(6\) units apart, and the vertices \((3, 3)\), \((3, -7)\) are \(10\) units apart.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
Horizontal: \(\frac{(x-h)^2}{a^2} + \frac{(y-k)^2}{b^2} = 1\), foci \((h \pm c, k)\), vertices \((h \pm a, k)\), co-vertices \((h, k \pm b)\), directrices \(x = h \pm \frac{a}{e}\).
Vertical: \(\frac{(x-h)^2}{b^2} + \frac{(y-k)^2}{a^2} = 1\), foci \((h, k \pm c)\), vertices \((h, k \pm a)\), co-vertices \((h \pm b, k)\), directrices \(y = k \pm \frac{a}{e}\).
From a general equation: complete the squares, divide to get 1 on the right, then read \(h\), \(k\), \(a\), \(b\).
From given data: find the centre, the direction of the major axis, \(a\) and \(c\); then \(b^2 = a^2 - c^2\).

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
Forgetting to add the centre: for centre \((2, -3)\) the foci are \((2, -3 \pm \sqrt{7})\), not \((0, \pm\sqrt{7})\).
Writing the directrices of a translated ellipse as \(y = \pm\frac{a}{e}\); they are \(y = k \pm \frac{a}{e}\).
When completing the square with a coefficient outside, subtracting 4 instead of \(16 \times 4 = 64\).
